questions.q: In the lesson's measured stage timings for one hybrid iteration (total ~38,361 ms), what fraction of total time was queue wait?
options: About 99.1%, making queue wait by far the dominant cost in iteration latency
About 50%, split roughly evenly with QPU execution time
About 10%, with most time spent in classical pre/post-processing
0%, since queue wait only applies to batched submissions
questions.explain: 38,000ms of queue wait out of a 38,361ms total is about 99.1% -- QPU execution (40ms) and classical pre/post-processing (21ms combined) are a rounding error by comparison.

questions.q: What does batching 17 parameter-shift circuit evaluations into one program-set submission actually reduce, according to the lesson?
options: The number of SEPARATE queue waits paid (all 17 share one queue wait instead of each paying its own), not the number of circuit evaluations themselves
The number of circuit evaluations needed, from 17 down to 1
The accuracy of the gradient estimate
The per-shot price charged by the provider
questions.explain: Batching doesn't change how many circuit evaluations are needed (still 17) -- it changes how many times you wait in queue, since all 17 share a single queue wait instead of 17 separate ones, producing the ~16.8x speedup shown in the lesson.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked comparison, roughly how much faster is the batched approach than the unbatched approach for one iteration (17 evaluations)?
options: About 16.8x faster (roughly 42.75 sec batched vs. roughly 717,150 ms / ~11.95 min unbatched)
About 2x faster
Exactly the same speed either way
The unbatched approach is actually faster
questions.explain: 717,150 ms / 42,750 ms ~= 16.8 -- batching collapses 17 separate queue waits into one shared queue wait, producing a large wall-clock speedup with identical total QPU compute.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend structuring orchestration code as an explicit, persisted job state machine instead of a blocking submit-then-while-loop-poll call?
options: A blocking loop ties up an entire process for the full queue wait and loses track of in-flight jobs on a restart, while a persisted state machine lets one process manage many concurrent jobs and resume after a crash
State machines are required by all cloud quantum provider SDKs
Blocking loops are actually faster than state machines in every case
Job state has no effect on whether a crashed process can resume tracking a job
questions.explain: A blocking poll loop wastes process resources for the entire queue wait and has no way to recover job state after a crash. An explicit, persisted state machine (PENDING_SUBMIT -> QUEUED -> RUNNING -> ...) supports restart-safety and concurrent job handling, which matters at real workload scale.

questions.q: Given the stage timings in the lesson, which optimization would have the LEAST impact on total iteration latency?
options: Optimizing the 40ms QPU execution time or the ~21ms of classical pre/post-processing work
Reducing the number of separate queue waits paid via batching
Choosing a device with a shorter observed queue depth
Restructuring the submission strategy to share queue wait across multiple circuit evaluations
questions.explain: Since queue wait is ~99.1% of total time, shaving milliseconds off the 40ms execution time or 21ms of classical work has almost no effect on the overall 38-second iteration -- the leverage is entirely in reducing how often and how long you queue.
